title: 「已经没有简单答案，也没有现成剧本」——Secret Mode 以两条差异化路线下注
content:
"There is no easy answer anymore, there's no kind of playbook" – Secret Mode is hedging its bets with two very different pillars | GamesIndustry.biz

.
It's all smiles over at Secret Mode right now. Since
breaking free from Sumo Digital
(and its parent Tencent) last year, the newly independent UK publisher has been going great guns.
Speaking to
GamesIndustry.biz
at Gamescom, chief publishing officer James Schall says Secret Mode has seen "phenomenal growth" over the past 18 months. At the outset, they made a business plan leading up to 2030, he says, and "we smashed it within about four months."
James Schall
He adds that the separation from Sumo – aided by investment from Emona Capital – was relatively simple, and that Tencent has been "very helpful" throughout the process. "I couldn't believe how quickly the deal was done to extricate us from Sumo, and how positive that experience has been for everyone," he says.
The separation made sense on both sides. As Schall says, after
Sumo was purchased
by "the vast Tencent machine" in early 2022, there was a process where the Chinese giant was working out what to do with all the many companies within its portfolio. "[They] didn't need 18 different publishers, right?" That tallies with what Tencent's Yong-yi Zhu recently told
GamesIndustry.biz
, where the firm has been making decisions about
which companies fit with its long-term strategy
.
Ed Blincoe
But what about Secret Mode's strategy? As Schall and CEO Ed Blincoe explain, the publishing is targeting two pillars: "pure indie" titles, along with higher budget games like Star Wars: Galactic Racer. The hope is that investing in quality will help the publisher punch through.
As Schall says, in the current environment where
discoverability is only getting harder
, "it's almost impossible to sell a mediocre game", and even selling a "very, very good game" remains difficult. "There is no easy answer anymore, there's no kind of playbook. You just have to try and make yourself lucky by making the right decisions."
And some of those decisions involve investing in games that have already seen some success, but that have the potential to do much more.
Caretaker development
Secret Mode has placed a big bet on Star Wars Galactic Racer, due for release on October 6. Schall says the wishlists for the game are "phenomenal".
Blincoe says the game was "exceptional when we played it for the first time over 12 months ago, and it's only got better as we've gone through that period of time. We're really confident in the game."
Secret Mode is confident in the success of Star Wars: Galactic Racer  |
Image credit:
Fuse Games/Secret Mode
Galactic Racer has been developed by
new UK studio Fuse Games
, and Blincoe says Secret Mode signed it at the end of September last year, after convincing Emona Capital it was worth investing in. "We walked through the door and said we have this opportunity, we need to figure out how we can possibly fund it: they helped us find out how to fund it."
But the publisher's other high-budget investments are of a different nature. Secret Mode has taken on publishing duties for Fancy Games' Escape the Backrooms, which was initially released in Early Access in 2022,
as well as Anegar Games' Chained Together
, which came out in 2024.
Schall says co-op games like these – or friendslop titles to give them their much-maligned but now seemingly unshiftable modern moniker – cater to an audience that is used to being online. "They grew up during COVID, they're used to interacting on Twitch, and that's where they're hanging out with their mates," he says. "I think you can either just go, 'Yeah, it's viral, and it'll last for about four weeks', or we can iterate on it, and bring more things, and try and keep people within that home."
Chained Together sees friends attempting to escape hell while, as you guessed it, being chained together  |
Image credit:
Anegar Games/Lab42/Secret Mode
Blincoe says that in addition to publishing the games, Secret Mode is taking on the development of them via trusted partners – the
external development studio Blackbird Interactive
has already been working on Escape the Backrooms for a while. In addition, Secret Mode has
opened its own internal development studio in Sheffield
, which "will help to continue to make content for those games," says Blincoe.
He adds that both games sell "a good number of units each month" and pay for their own development. "And what we're seeing is new players coming in and wanting more, and the existing community wanting more content as well. So that's why we're trying to deliver that for them."
Secret Mode became the publisher for Escape the Backrooms in August 2025  |
Image credit:
Fancy Games/Blackbird Interactive/Secret Mode
This is a new 'caretaker development' model we're seeing in the games industry, where other parties are taking over the reins of existing titles when the original developers decide to move on, even though the game itself remains a going concern. French developer Evil Empire recently took over content development for Blobfish's hit game Brotato, and
the studio is actively looking for other titles it can help out on
.
Schall says there's a "number of opportunities with developers who have found success, and they've become a little bit trapped in their work from wanting to be creatively different, the community is very demanding, or they've just been very financially happy with their income and they want to go off and do something else. How do they do that? We've come along and helped individuals reset, re-find their love for their games, and we do the publishing stuff. Which is not easy, but we're very experienced at it, and we know great people to help us do new things."
The long tail
It's something Secret Mode has history with: Schall gives the example of
Wobbledogs
, which was created by Tom Astle, but was "stuck" in
